bib.title: "Why Should I Trust You?" Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier

question: How can the prediction of any black-box classifier be explained faithfully and interpretably so that users can decide whether to trust a prediction or a model?
hypothesis: Local, interpretable, model-agnostic explanations (plus a diverse set of representative ones) help users assess trust, choose between models and improve untrustworthy classifiers better than accuracy alone or baseline explainers.
contributions: LIME, an algorithm that can explain the predictions of any classifier or regressor in a faithful way, by approximating it locally with an interpretable model.
SP-LIME, a method that selects a set of representative instances with explanations to address the "trusting the model" problem, via submodular optimization.
Comprehensive evaluation with simulated and human subjects, measuring the impact of explanations on trust and associated tasks.

method.summary: LIME perturbs an instance in an interpretable binary representation (words present/absent, super-pixels on/off), labels perturbations with the black-box f, weights them by an exponential proximity kernel, and fits a K-sparse linear model (K-Lasso then least squares). SP-LIME greedily picks B instances whose explanations cover the most important features. Evaluated with simulated users on sentiment data and with Mechanical Turk and student subjects on 20 newsgroups and a husky/wolf image task.
method.task: post-hoc explanation of classifier predictions (text and image); trust assessment, model selection, feature engineering

models.name: LIME (sparse linear explainer)
models.architecture: K-sparse linear model over binary interpretable representation

other.kernel: pi_x(z)=exp(-D(x,z)^2/sigma^2); D cosine for text, L2 for images
other.K: 10 in simulated experiments; K=10 for Inception super-pixel example
other.feature selection: K-Lasso via regularization path then least squares
other.N: 15,000 samples in simulated experiments; 5000 in the timing example

other.budget B: 6 in human model-choice study; 10 in feature-engineering study

models.name: Decision tree, logistic regression (L2), nearest neighbours, SVM RBF, random forest (1000 trees, avg word2vec)
parzen
models.architecture: global Parzen-window approximation, top-K absolute gradients

models.name: greedy
models.architecture: greedily remove features contributing most to predicted class until prediction changes or K features

inference.samples: N=15,000 perturbations per explanation (simulated experiments); trust experiment averaged over 100 runs; model-selection simulation 800 runs; 100 MTurk users per setting; feature engineering 10 initial subjects x 5 users per later round, 250 final classifiers; husky/wolf 27 subjects

parameters.sigma: hyper-parameters for parzen and LIME set by cross validation; value not given
parameters.noisy features: 10 artificial features appear in 10% of examples in one class and 20% in the other on train/val; 10% each class on test
parameters.classifier pairs: random forests of 30 trees trained until validation accuracy within 0.1% but test accuracy differs by at least 5%

other.timing: explaining random forests with 1000 trees, N=5000, scikit-learn on a laptop: under 3 seconds; Inception image prediction around 10 minutes

metrics.name: Recall on gold features
metrics.definition: fraction of the (at most 10) gold features of an interpretable classifier recovered by the explanation, averaged over test instances

metrics.name: F1 of trustworthiness
metrics.definition: F1 on trustworthy predictions of a simulated user versus an oracle that marks a prediction untrustworthy if it changes when untrustworthy features are removed

metrics.name: % correct choice
metrics.definition: share of runs/users choosing the classifier with higher real-world (held-out/religion) accuracy

metrics.name: Real world accuracy
metrics.definition: accuracy on the religion dataset of classifiers retrained after subjects delete words

eval.protocol: Simulated users: averages over 100 runs (trust) and 800 runs (model selection), trust results significant at p = 0.01 (test not named). Human: Mechanical Turk workers (non-experts), graduate students with at least one ML course for husky/wolf, 3 independent evaluators with majority vote.

limits: Faithfulness is only checked on interpretable models whose gold features are known (sparse LR, decision trees, <=10 features); no check on black boxes is reported.
Trust experiments simulate users by randomly marking 25% of features untrustworthy and by injected noise features, so results are artificial.
Husky vs Wolf study is small (27 graduate students) and the classifier was trained to be bad on 20 hand-picked images; authors concede 'our sample size is small'.
Pick step for images is not solved (future work).
Sparse linear G may not give a faithful explanation if the model is highly non-linear locally; sepia-toned example shows interpretable representations can be too weak.
K is fixed (10 or 6), choice of kernel width and superpixel algorithm not specified; theoretical sample-size properties unexplored; Inception explanation takes about 10 minutes per prediction.
Human results compare against greedy, not against other published explainers; significance test not named.

terms.definition: whether a user trusts an individual prediction sufficiently to take some action based on it
whether the user trusts a model to behave in reasonable ways if deployed
explanation must correspond to how the model behaves in the vicinity of the instance being predicted
x' in {0,1}^d' binary vector of presence of words or super-pixels, distinct from model features

code.snippet: xi(x) = argmin_{g in G} L(f, g, pi_x) + Omega(g)
L(f,g,pi_x) = sum_{z,z' in Z} pi_x(z) (f(z) - g(z'))^2
